html:
A hilltop site in south-eastern Turkey, near Şanlıurfa, with the oldest known monumental buildings in the world, raised between about 9500 and 8000 BCE. It is older than this chart, which starts at 3300 BCE.

Its builders set T-shaped limestone pillars, up to 5.5 metres tall and many tonnes in weight, in round enclosures with two larger pillars at the centre. Many are carved with foxes, boars, snakes, cranes and scorpions; some have arms and hands, so the pillars may stand for people or spirits.

The people who built it had no pottery, no metal and no farm animals. They hunted gazelle and gathered wild grain. That upset the older view that large building came only after farming and villages. Klaus Schmidt, who dug here from 1995, called it a temple built by hunters; later digs found houses, cisterns and grinding stones, so people probably lived here too.
